symptoms: Small dark spots form first on the older leaves near the ground.
Leaf spots are round and brown and can grow up to half an inch across.
Badly infected leaves turn brown and may fall off or cling dead to the stem.
treatment: Wash and sanitise tools after touching infected plants.
If a fungicide is needed, apply it when the weather favours the disease and alternate between chemical families so the fungus does not become insensitive.
prevention: Space plants so air can move through them and keep the foliage dry.
Remove or bury infected plants at the end of the season.
Rotate crops: do not plant potato or tomato in the same place for at least two years.
potato___Early_blight.severity: Can severely limit yield on susceptible varieties.

sources.title: Early blight in tomato and potato, University of Minnesota Extension

symptoms: Large dark brown blotches with a green-grey edge appear on leaves and are not held in by the leaf veins.
The infection moves through leaflets and leaf stalks, leaving large sections of dry brown foliage.
In cool wet weather whole fields turn brown and wilted, as if hit by frost.
Infected tubers become discoloured (brown, red or purple) and soft.
treatment: If only a few plants are infected, remove them, disc them under or kill them so the disease does not spread through the field.
Fungicides must be ones that work on water molds, and they work only when applied before infection.
Rotate or tank-mix fungicide groups to avoid resistance.
prevention: Control volunteer potato plants, which can grow from infected tubers.
Manage cull piles so they do not become a source of infection.
Plant where no potato, tomato, pepper or eggplant has grown for the past 3 to 4 years.
Remove or bury plants at the end of the season.
potato___Late_blight.severity: Can cause total crop failure if left untreated. It favours cool (60 to 70 °F), damp weather; long hot dry spells can stop its spread.
